column2: Core Idea: "tradition, descending from Petrarch, created a 14-line form"
column5: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonnet ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilian_School (Giacomo da Lentini, Sicilian court c. 1230s; Petrarch popularized, did not invent)
column6: created a 14-line form -> "used a 14-line form, first developed by 13th-century Sicilian court poets,"

column2: Core Idea + q:3 explanation + Explainer: essay "the dominant vehicle for Enlightenment intellectual expression" / "preferred form"
column5: Overstated: major Enlightenment works were treatises, the Encyclopedie, letters, dialogues and novels; the periodical essay (Addison, Steele) and Hume's Essays were important but not dominant. https://ebooks.inflibnet.ac.in/engp02/chapter/addison-and-steele/
column6: Core Idea -> "an important vehicle for later intellectual expression, including for many Enlightenment writers"; q:3 explanation -> "an important vehicle ... used by writers such as Addison, Steele and Hume alongside treatises, letters and encyclopedias" (dropped "far more influential than treatises"); Explainer "the preferred form for Enlightenment thinkers precisely because" -> "a favored form for many Enlightenment writers because". q:3 answer (true) unchanged and still correct.

column2: Core Idea "without grammatical organization"; q:2 T/F "requires abandoning grammar" answer true; also q:0 option/explanation and Explainer para 3 repeat the claim
column5: Woolf (Mrs Dalloway) renders thought in grammatical sentences via free indirect discourse; only some passages drop syntax, e.g. Penelope episode of Ulysses, eight sentences with almost no punctuation. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Bloom
column6: Core Idea -> "without a narrator's logical ordering, sometimes loosening or dropping conventional grammar and punctuation"; q:0 correct option -> "without imposing a narrator's logical order" and explanation adjusted (answer index 2 unchanged); q:2 answer true -> false with new explanation; Explainer "operates through abandoning conventional grammar" -> "operates by loosening conventional logical ordering and, in some writers, conventional grammar", "coherent sentences" -> "a narrator's orderly account"

column5: Romanticism is widely described as partly a reaction against industrialization/the Industrial Revolution, so the distractor is arguably correct (see Wikipedia Romanticism summary via https://www.doc.surf/wiki/romanticism)
column6: Replaced distractor with "Twentieth-century modernist experimentation"; answer index 1 and explanation unchanged

column2: elevated spiritual longing ... above carnal satisfaction; "Possession or physical satisfaction would diminish the love"; "all subsequent European lyric poetry" / "Every subsequent love poet"
column5: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtly_love (scholars split on chaste vs sexual readings; Lazar: adulterous sexual love; poems range from bawdy to near-platonic; Lewis: "Adultery"); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comtessa_de_Dia (Estat ai wishes to hold her knight naked in her arms); influence on Sicilian School, Dante, Petrarch, Petrarchism
column6: Core Idea rewritten to "ennobling, often unrequited desire that prized refinement, patience and service, though many songs also openly desire physical union" and "shaped much later European lyric poetry"; q:0 correct option -> "Ennobling, often unrequited desire expressed through refined devotion and service" with new explanation (answer index 1 unchanged); q:2 and q:3 explanations softened; q:4 explanation dropped "Requital would actually diminish the love"; Explainer paras 1, 3 and 6 softened ("not primarily about physical desire", "the paradox that would define", "elevation of spiritual over carnal love", "Every subsequent love poet" -> "Many later love poets, including Dante and Petrarch")

column2: Explainer: "something unprecedented in medieval European culture: a sophisticated ... tradition composed entirely in a vernacular"
column5: Old English poetry dates from the 7th century (Caedmon's Hymn), long before the troubadours (c. 1100). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English_literature
column6: Removed "unprecedented"; now "a sophisticated, artistically ambitious lyric tradition composed entirely in a Romance vernacular", adds "Earlier vernacular traditions existed, such as Old English poetry, but in the Romance-speaking world Latin was..."; "Vernacular languages were considered crude" -> "were widely considered less fit for serious art or learning"

column2: Explainer: "For many educated Victorians, faith became impossible" / "a post-Christian age"
column5: Victorian Britain remained largely Christian; 1851 census attendance high by modern standards; Larsen argues the crisis was more read about than lived. https://victorianweb.org/religion/larsen6.html ; https://www.historytoday.com/archive/religion-victorian-city
column6: For many educated Victorians, faith became impossible to maintain -> "For some educated Victorians, faith became impossible to maintain, and many more felt it shaken"; "post-Christian age" -> "age of religious doubt"

column2: Explainer: "Dante had done this with classical epic form"; "shifted cultural emphasis from religious salvation to secular accomplishment"
column5: Commedia is in terza rima and reflects the medieval worldview, but Dante took Virgil as his model (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_Comedy). Most humanists were Christian; Kristeller and Hankins reject a secular reading (https://www.sacredarchitecture.org/articles/the_myth_of_renaissance_secular_humanism ; https://encyclopedia.com/history/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/humanists-and-humanism)
column6: Dante had done this with classical epic form -> "Dante, a late medieval forerunner, had already taken Virgil's epic as a model for his Italian Commedia"; "This shifted cultural emphasis from religious salvation to secular accomplishment" -> "This gave new weight to earthly accomplishment alongside religious salvation" (now consistent with q:3)

column2: Explainer: "what realism and modernism tried to hide: that representation is always constructed"
column5: Modernism was highly self-conscious about form; Gide's The Counterfeiters (1925) is an early metafictional novel-within-a-novel. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Counterfeiters_(novel)
column6: what realism and modernism tried to hide -> "what realist conventions tend to hide"

column2: Core Idea: realist novelists "developed new formal techniques ... free indirect discourse"; Explainer "developed technical innovations"
column5: Austen (from Sense and Sensibility, 1811) and Goethe were among the first novelists to use free indirect speech consistently; Flaubert later exploited it. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_indirect_speech
column6: Core Idea "developed new formal techniques" -> "refined and extended formal techniques" and added "already used by earlier writers such as Jane Austen"; Explainer "developed technical innovations" -> "refined techniques"

column2: Explainer (check.tsv note): "Postmodernism proved that skepticism toward truth need not lead to nihilism"
column5: Interpretive claim stated as a proven fact; a literary movement cannot prove a philosophical thesis. Reasoning only.
column6: Postmodernism proved that -> "Postmodern writers set out to show that"
